introduction: In the summer of 1848 some eighty followers of the Báb met in gardens at the hamlet of Badasht. They arrived keeping the law of Islam; they left knowing that a new dispensation had begun; and the sign of it was Táhirih appearing among them without her veil. The guide gathers recollections of the gathering: Bahá’u’lláh’s quiet direction of it, the shock, those who fled and said they had been deceived, and what it cost the woman at its centre. The Gospels know the moment when new wine bursts old bottles, and the hard saying after which many “walked no more with him”. They also preserve the sentence that not a jot of the law shall pass, which is the question Badasht forces. Paul’s figure of the veil taken away, and Wollstonecraft on the end of blind obedience, stand beside Táhirih’s act.
questions: New wine and old bottles; not one jot shall pass. How do readings 5 and 12 present the break with the earlier law: as rupture, as fulfilment, or as both?
Why did the announcement take the form of an act, a woman’s unveiling, and not only a statement?
“This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” What do the accounts of those who fled (reading 9) suggest about what a community owes to those who cannot follow a change?
Reading 11 records what Táhirih’s family did. How should the cost borne by particular people enter the telling of a founding event?

outside.why: From the beginning the believers looked to Bahá’u’lláh for guidance, though he held no rank among them. The people were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Bahá’u’lláh is said to have tested souls in the early days. The Bible’s great test: Abraham stretched forth his hand, and was stopped: now I know that thou fearest God.
Believers gather in a garden, and something new is declared. When the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.
Until then the Bábís had kept the rules of Islam; now a new order was announced. Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break.
The first sign that an older law no longer bound: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.

Jesus also said: think not that I am come to destroy the law; till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law. Badasht made the break visible in a day. How does a community tell fulfilment from destruction while it is happening?

Táhirih appeared unveiled before the men, and some fled. Paul uses the veil as a figure for the old reading of scripture: when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away. Here the figure was enacted by a woman, at her own risk. What did the act say that words had not?
Wollstonecraft, half a century earlier and a world away: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
One who fled Badasht went about saying he had been deceived. From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
The reason given in the Gospel is the one given here: this is an hard saying; who can hear it?
Her husband, sons and family rose against her. He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.

An account of the conference is called accurate but not complete, and is supplemented. Luke: it seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order.
